```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4,
                      out.width = "100%")
library(skellam)
set.seed(20261108)
```

## What this vignette checks

If $Y_1 \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda_1)$ and $Y_2 \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda_2)$
are independent, their difference $X = Y_1 - Y_2$ has the Skellam distribution,

$$
P(X = x) = e^{-(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)} \left(\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2}\right)^{x/2}
I_{|x|}\!\left(2\sqrt{\lambda_1\lambda_2}\right), \qquad x \in \mathbb{Z},
$$

with mean $\lambda_1 - \lambda_2$ and variance $\lambda_1 + \lambda_2$. This vignette
checks, with numbers rather than by eye, that the functions of the package agree with
that definition and with each other:

1. `dskellam` against an exact sum over Poisson probabilities;
2. `pskellam` against cumulative sums of `dskellam`, and `qskellam` as its inverse;
3. `rskellam` against `dskellam` with a goodness-of-fit test;
4. `skellam.mle` and `skellam.reg` against known parameters in simulated data.

Every random number below is drawn after `set.seed(20261108)`, so the output is the
same each time the vignette is built.

## 1. The probability mass function

By definition, $P(X = x) = \sum_k P(Y_1 = k + x)\,P(Y_2 = k)$. Summing that series
directly is slow but exact, which makes it a good reference.

```{r pmf-exact}
pmf_by_sum <- function(x, l1, l2) {
  k <- max(0, -x):(abs(x) + 200 + 20 * (l1 + l2))
  sum(dpois(k + x, l1) * dpois(k, l2))
}
x <- -10:15
for (L in list(c(1.5, 0.5), c(12, 8))) {
  ref <- vapply(x, pmf_by_sum, 0, l1 = L[1], l2 = L[2])
  cat(sprintf("lambda = (%g, %g): largest relative difference %.1e\n",
              L[1], L[2], max(abs(dskellam(x, L[1], L[2]) / ref - 1))))
}
```

The probabilities also add up to one, including at rates far beyond what the
series above can handle quickly:

```{r pmf-mass}
for (L in list(c(1.5, 0.5), c(12, 8), c(1e4, 1e4), c(1e6, 1e6))) {
  s <- sqrt(sum(L)); m <- L[1] - L[2]
  x <- seq(floor(m - 30 * s), ceiling(m + 30 * s))
  cat(sprintf("lambda = (%g, %g): 1 - sum = %.1e\n", L[1], L[2],
              1 - sum(dskellam(x, L[1], L[2]))))
}
```

When one rate is zero the distribution is a Poisson, or a Poisson turned upside down:

```{r pmf-poisson}
all.equal(dskellam(0:10, 5, 0), dpois(0:10, 5))
all.equal(dskellam(-(0:10), 0, 5), dpois(0:10, 5))
```

## 2. Distribution and quantile functions

`pskellam(x)` should equal the running sum of `dskellam` up to `x`, and the two tails
should add up to one.

```{r cdf}
l1 <- 12; l2 <- 8
x <- -40:50
max(abs(pskellam(x, l1, l2) - cumsum(dskellam(x, l1, l2))))
max(abs(pskellam(x, l1, l2) + pskellam(x, l1, l2, lower.tail = FALSE) - 1))
```

For a discrete distribution the quantile function returns the smallest integer $x$
with $P(X \le x) \ge p$. Feeding a value of the distribution function back in must
therefore return the same $x$, on both tails and on the log scale:

```{r quantile}
x <- -15:25
all(qskellam(pskellam(x, l1, l2), l1, l2) == x)
all(qskellam(pskellam(x, l1, l2, lower.tail = FALSE), l1, l2, lower.tail = FALSE) == x)
all(qskellam(pskellam(x, l1, l2, log.p = TRUE), l1, l2, log.p = TRUE) == x)
qskellam(c(0, 0.025, 0.5, 0.975, 1), l1, l2)
```

## 3. Random generation

`rskellam` draws the difference of two Poisson variates. We compare the observed
frequencies of 20,000 draws with the probabilities from `dskellam`, pooling the
sparse tails so every cell expects at least 5 observations.

```{r random}
N <- 20000
lambda1 <- 1.5; lambda2 <- 0.5
z <- rskellam(N, lambda1, lambda2)
c(mean = mean(z), expected = lambda1 - lambda2)
c(variance = var(z), expected = lambda1 + lambda2)

lo <- qskellam(0.001, lambda1, lambda2); hi <- qskellam(0.999, lambda1, lambda2)
cells <- lo:hi
prob <- dskellam(cells, lambda1, lambda2)
prob[1] <- pskellam(lo, lambda1, lambda2)                                 # all x <= lo
prob[length(prob)] <- pskellam(hi - 1, lambda1, lambda2, lower.tail = FALSE)  # all x >= hi
obs <- table(factor(pmin(pmax(z, lo), hi), levels = cells))
chisq.test(obs, p = prob)
```

```{r random-plot, fig.cap = "Observed frequencies of 20,000 draws (bars) and the expected frequencies from dskellam (points)."}
plot(cells, as.vector(obs), type = "h", lwd = 6, col = "grey70",
     xlab = "x", ylab = "Frequency", main = "")
points(cells, N * prob, pch = 19, col = "#0072B2")
legend("topright", c("rskellam", "N * dskellam"), lwd = c(6, NA), pch = c(NA, 19),
       col = c("grey70", "#0072B2"), bty = "n")
```

## 4. Estimation

### Maximum likelihood for a sample

```{r mle}
x <- rpois(2000, 12) - rpois(2000, 8)
fit <- skellam.mle(x)
fit$param
```

At the maximum the fitted mean equals the sample mean, and the estimates are close
to the true values (12, 8). Samples whose variance does not exceed the absolute
mean cannot come from a Skellam with two positive rates; the estimate then puts one
rate at zero instead of returning a negative rate:

```{r mle-boundary}
skellam.mle(rep(3, 50))$param
skellam.mle(c(rep(2, 45), rep(3, 5)))$param
```

### Regression

`skellam.reg(y, x)` lets both rates depend on covariates through a log link. For
$y = Y_1 - Y_2$, `param1` describes the rate of the counts that are added
($\lambda_1$) and `param2` the rate of the counts that are subtracted ($\lambda_2$).

```{r reg}
n <- 1000
covariate <- rnorm(n)
y <- rpois(n, exp(1 + 0.5 * covariate)) - rpois(n, exp(-0.5 + 0.3 * covariate))
reg <- skellam.reg(y, covariate)
round(reg$param1, 3)   # true values 1 and 0.5
round(reg$param2, 3)   # true values -0.5 and 0.3
```
